evidence.label: Weak and strong normalization in pure type systems

headline: Claims that in every pure type system, if every legal term can finish computing, then every way of computing finishes.
scope: All pure type systems, with any sorts and possibly nonfunctional axioms and rules, under beta reduction including inside type annotations.
plain: Pure type systems are a family of typed programming languages that also serve as logics. A program is weakly normalizing if some way of running it stops, and strongly normalizing if every way stops. The paper claims that when every legal program in a system has some stopping run, every run of every legal program stops. This settles the beta form of a conjecture from the early 1990s. A Lean proof checks the main theorem.
doesNot: This does not say that one single term with a normal form always terminates, and it says nothing about adding eta reduction.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Herman Geuvers, statement of the conjecture in his thesis
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a well-known open question in type theory, which underlies proof assistants.

explanation:
Start with a small program in the lambda calculus, the core language behind functional programming. Let K be the function that takes x and always returns y. Let Ω be the term (λx.xx)(λx.xx), which applies a function to itself. Running Ω one step gives back Ω exactly, so it never stops. Now look at K applied to Ω. Run the outer call first, and you get y in one step. Run the inner Ω first, and you loop forever. So this term can finish, but it does not have to.

A term is weakly normalizing if some sequence of beta steps reaches a normal form, a term with nothing left to compute. It is strongly normalizing if every such sequence is finite. A beta step is the basic computing move: plug an argument into a function body. Type systems rule out terms like Ω. A pure type system fixes a set of sorts, such as "type" and "kind", and rules for building function types. Related type systems underlie proof assistants such as Coq and Lean.

Barendregt, Geuvers and Klop conjectured that for these systems the two notions agree at the level of the whole system. Geuvers stated it in his 1993 thesis[1]. Earlier work proved it for restricted families. For example, Sørensen used program translations for some systems without dependent types[2]. Those translations need particular rules to be present, so they do not reach every system[3]. That is the obstacle: a general system may have no hierarchy of sorts and no tidy rules.

The paper claims the full beta version. In any pure type system, if every legal term in every valid context is weakly normalizing, then every such term is strongly normalizing[4]. Steps inside type annotations count too[5]. No functionality assumption on the axioms or rules is needed. The claim is about the whole system. It does not say that one term with a normal form must always stop[6]. So K applied to Ω is no counterexample. In a weakly normalizing system it cannot be legal, because Ω has no normal form. The proof first cuts the system down to finitely many sorts and rules[7]. It then adapts the Tait–Girard method of reducibility candidates[8]. That method attaches to each type a set of terms that are known to terminate.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of the main theorem. It covers any specification, arbitrary sorts, nonfunctional axioms and rules, and reduction inside annotations. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: The main theorem has a Lean proof and settles the beta form of a known conjecture. The eta form is not addressed. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A minimal programming language where everything is a function and computing means plugging arguments into function bodies.
One computing step: replace a function applied to an argument by the function body with the argument plugged in.
A term with no beta step left to take.
Some sequence of beta steps reaches a normal form.
Every sequence of beta steps is finite.
A family of typed lambda calculi given by a set of sorts, axioms between sorts, and rules for which function types may be formed.
A term that appears in some derivable typing judgment of the system.
